title: 11 Questions You Must Answer Before Leaving Your Corporate Job
author: Ethan Evans
source: Level Up with Ethan Evans (levelupwithethanevans.substack.com), August 25, 2026
summary: Former Amazon VP Ethan Evans, drawing on a live coaching session with strategic advisor Kristin Cruz, lays out eleven pressure-test questions for anyone considering leaving a corporate job to start their own business. He organizes the questions around reversibility (can you return if it fails), actual financial and logistical constraints, and a hard-nosed marketing distinction between being a 'vitamin' (nice to have) versus a 'painkiller' (an urgent problem people will pay to fix). He stresses that most new entrepreneurs describe their offering backward, starting from their own skills rather than the customer's problem, and that solo or small consulting practices are inherently 'lumpy,' where losing one client can erase a quarter of revenue overnight. Evans closes by warning that leaving corporate means inheriting every function a company quietly handled for you, from bookkeeping to marketing to sales, and that the decision should be made with clear eyes about that full workload rather than nostalgia for the parts of the old job you enjoyed.
points: Evans's central reframe for solo entrepreneurs is the 'vitamin vs. painkiller' distinction: offerings that are merely nice to have get price resistance, while offerings that solve an urgent, expensive problem command real money.

He flags that most new entrepreneurs describe their business backward, starting from their own credentials ('I'm an experienced operator') rather than the customer's problem, and gives a concrete reframe example to fix it.

His financial-planning warning about 'lumpiness' is stark: in a small, high-touch consulting practice, losing one of four or five clients can instantly erase 25% of revenue, requiring a deliberate cash buffer.

Evans's 'one-way door vs. two-way door' framing (borrowed from Amazon) reduces the reversibility question to one concrete test: can you return to a similar corporate role after six months to a year if the business doesn't work, and is your network intact enough to make that possible?
quotes: If you leave, try something for six months or a year, and discover that you hate it or can't make enough money, can you go back? For many people, the answer is yes. This is comforting.
Those are all valuable capabilities, but to be frank, no one cares. The customer is always thinking about their problem, that's where you need to start.
If what you are selling is merely nice to have, you are a vitamin. If you are solving an immediate and expensive problem, you are closer to a painkiller. The money is closer to the pain.
Lose one client and you just lost 25% of your business. Gain one and your workload just increased 25%. Small businesses can be incredibly lumpy.
When you work inside a large corporation, entire departments quietly make your life easier. When you start your own company, all of those jobs become yours.

It means deciding what you sell, why anyone should buy it, how they will find you, how the economics will work, how you will handle the inevitable ups and downs, and who will do every piece of work your old company quietly handled for you.
